title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
statement: You get two sorted arrays, either of which may be empty (but not both). Find the median of all their items together, as if they were merged. The median is the middle item, or the average of the two middle items when the count is even. Aim for O(log(min(m, n))).

example.caption: Merged, the items are 1 2 3 4. The count is even, so the median is the average of 2 and 3.

idea.sentence: Cut both arrays so the left sides together hold half the items. The cut is right when every left item is no bigger than every right item, and you only need to check four items next to the cuts.

jargon.plain: The value in the middle once everything is sorted. For an even count it is the mean of the two middle values.
A cut that splits an array into a left part and a right part. Here one cut in each array, together giving the merged left half.

watch.inputHint: Two arguments: two sorted arrays, e.g. [1,3] and [2,4]. One may be empty.

compare.bruteLabel: Merge both arrays, take the middle
compare.optimalLabel: Binary search the cut in the shorter array

rows.name: Merge
rows.note: Merge into one sorted array and read the middle. Simple and correct, but linear.

rows.name: Merge with counters
rows.note: Walk two pointers up to the middle without storing the merge. Less memory, same time.

rows.name: Partition binary search
rows.note: Only the cut in the shorter array is searched. The cut in the other array follows from it.

fast.takeaway: You never merge. Guess where the median's left half ends in the shorter array, and four comparisons tell you which way to move.

stages.title: Shorter first
stages.note: Make a the shorter array, then work out how many items belong on the left: (total + 1) / 2.

stages.title: Range of cuts
stages.note: The cut in a can sit at any position from 0 to len(a). That range is what we search.

stages.title: Cut both
stages.note: Cut a after i items. Cut b after half - i, so the two left parts hold half the items together.

stages.title: Check the neighbours
stages.note: a's left item must not beat b's right item, and b's left item must not beat a's right item. If not, move the cut in a.

stages.title: Read the median
stages.note: Odd count: the biggest left item. Even count: average it with the smallest right item.

edges.title: One array is empty
edges.why: The only cut in a is 0. Its left and right neighbours are minus and plus infinity, so b alone decides the median.

edges.title: Odd total
edges.why: The left side has (3 + 1) / 2 = 2 items. The median is just the biggest of the left side.

edges.title: No overlap
edges.why: All of a is on the left. The cut in a is at the very end and aRight is plus infinity, so the average uses b's first item.

edges.title: All duplicates
edges.why: Checks use > not >=. Equal neighbours are fine, so the first cut that is tried is accepted.

gotchas.text: Use -Infinity and Infinity as sentinels, and never do arithmetic on them. In the even case only real numbers are averaged, because both sides always hold at least one item when total >= 2.
(total + 1) / 2 is fractional for odd totals in JS. Wrap it in Math.floor, or the cut position is something like 2.5.
math.MinInt and math.MaxInt work as sentinels because the inputs are far smaller. Never add them or negate them, or you overflow.
Integer division of the sum gives a wrong answer for even totals. Convert to float64 before dividing by 2: float64(x+y) / 2.
Search the shorter array. That is what keeps j = half - i inside 0..len(b). Searching the longer one can give a negative cut in the other array.

recap.key: Cut both arrays so the left halves hold half the items. The cut is valid when the left items of each side are no bigger than the right items of the other.
moves: Make a the shorter array. half = (total + 1) / 2
Cut a after i items and b after half - i
aLeft > bRight: move the cut left. bLeft > aRight: move it right
Median: max of the lefts, or averaged with the min of the rights
